definition: Computer systems designed to perform tasks that can require human-like judgment, such as recognizing patterns or processing language.
example: A navigation app predicts traffic and suggests a route.
commonMistake: Assuming every automated or internet-connected device is AI.
learningTip: Ask what task the system performs and whether it uses patterns, rules, or predictions.

definition: A way to build systems that learn patterns from examples and use those patterns to make predictions or decisions.
example: A spam filter learns signals associated with unwanted messages.
commonMistake: Thinking learning means the system understands or remembers like a person.
learningTip: Separate the data, the task, and the prediction when describing a machine-learning system.

definition: An AI system built to perform one task or a limited set of related tasks rather than general human activities.
example: A speech-to-text tool can transcribe audio without being able to plan a holiday.
commonMistake: Treating strong performance in one task as proof of general intelligence.
learningTip: Name the boundary of an AI tool: what it can do and what it was not designed to do.

definition: Meaningful human review and responsibility for an AI-supported process or decision.
example: A teacher reviews an AI-generated learning recommendation before acting on it.
commonMistake: Assuming a person is providing oversight merely because their name appears on the process.
learningTip: Look for a real opportunity to question, correct, or stop the system.

definition: AI that creates new text, images, audio, video, or code from learned patterns and an instruction.
example: A writing assistant drafts three versions of an event announcement.
commonMistake: Assuming generated means copied exactly from one known source.
learningTip: Describe both the requested input and the generated output when explaining a use case.

definition: Examples and information used to teach a model patterns that help it perform a task.
example: Labeled images can help a vision model distinguish different objects.
commonMistake: Treating training data as a perfect, complete collection of truth.
learningTip: Ask whether the training examples represent the task and the people affected by it.

definition: An instruction or input that tells a generative AI system what task to perform or what content to create.
example: Write a five-bullet summary for a new employee using the notes below.
commonMistake: Expecting a vague prompt to contain all the context and decisions the model needs.
learningTip: Add the task, audience, relevant context, constraints, and desired format.

definition: A person checking generated content for accuracy, suitability, safety, and fit before it is used.
example: An editor corrects an AI draft and confirms every event detail before publishing.
commonMistake: Skipping review because the output is only called a draft.
learningTip: Review the claims and the consequences of using them, not just the writing style.

definition: A model trained on language examples that generates text by estimating likely continuations in context.
example: A chat assistant uses the conversation and a new question to draft a reply.
commonMistake: Calling an LLM a live search engine or a perfect fact database.
learningTip: Remember: language fluency shows learned patterns, not guaranteed truth or human awareness.

definition: The process of estimating which token is likely to come next based on learned patterns and current context.
example: After The capital of France is, Paris is a likely continuation.
commonMistake: Thinking the next-token process is the same as checking the answer against reality.
learningTip: Use likely continuation to explain how text is generated, then discuss verification separately.

definition: The input and conversation information available to the model for generating the current response.
example: A request to use a supplied glossary changes how an LLM explains a technical term.
commonMistake: Assuming the model automatically knows every private or current fact that was not supplied.
learningTip: Provide relevant source material and state which parts should guide the answer.

definition: Language that sounds likely or well-formed but has not necessarily been verified as true.
example: An LLM gives a polished but nonexistent book citation.
commonMistake: Using confidence, detail, or good grammar as evidence.
learningTip: Treat important names, dates, numbers, and citations as claims to verify.

definition: A unit of processed text that can be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment.
example: A long word may be split into several tokens before a model processes it.
commonMistake: Assuming one token always equals one complete word.
learningTip: Think of tokens as the model's text units rather than ordinary word counts.

definition: The amount of tokenized information a model can process together for a current interaction.
example: A long document and a requested answer must fit within the available context capacity.
commonMistake: Assuming a larger window makes unrelated information useful.
learningTip: Keep high-value context and the task clear even when the system supports many tokens.

definition: Information that directly helps the model complete the current task accurately and appropriately.
example: Providing the current policy section instead of an entire unrelated chat history.
commonMistake: Adding more text simply because more context sounds safer.
learningTip: Ask whether each piece of context changes what a good answer should say or do.

definition: The limited token capacity shared by the current input and the response the model needs to generate.
example: Removing repeated notes leaves room for the model to produce the requested detailed summary.
commonMistake: Using all available input space and leaving too little room for the answer.
learningTip: Plan the response length as well as the input length when designing a prompt.

definition: An instruction and supporting context that describes a task for an AI system.
example: Summarize these notes for a new employee in five plain-language bullets.
commonMistake: Writing a broad request and expecting the model to infer every requirement.
learningTip: Start with a verb that names the task, then add audience, source, constraints, and format.

definition: A boundary in a prompt that controls length, tone, scope, required content, or output format.
example: Use no more than 80 words and include exactly three action items.
commonMistake: Assuming a constraint proves that the output is accurate.
learningTip: Use constraints to shape the result, then use sources and review to check it.

definition: The people the output is intended to help or communicate with.
example: Explain tokens to a first-time AI learner using a familiar everyday analogy.
commonMistake: Using the same vocabulary and depth for beginners and specialists.
learningTip: Name the audience and their prior knowledge so the model can adapt the explanation.

definition: A requested response shape such as bullets, headings, a table, or a fixed set of fields.
example: Return a table with task, owner, deadline, and source note columns.
commonMistake: Treating the requested shape as proof that each field contains a supported value.
learningTip: Add an unknown or needs-review value for information the source does not contain.

definition: An invented, inaccurate, or unsupported AI output presented as though it were reliable.
example: A chatbot creates a detailed but nonexistent citation.
commonMistake: Defining hallucination as any answer that is incomplete or stylistically awkward.
learningTip: Look for claims that can be checked, especially specific names, dates, numbers, and sources.

definition: Checking an AI claim against a trustworthy source, evidence, or qualified reviewer before relying on it.
example: Confirming a legal deadline on an official government website.
commonMistake: Treating a second identical AI answer as independent evidence.
learningTip: Choose the source based on the consequence and domain of the claim.

definition: A limitation or lack of confidence that should be made visible when evidence is incomplete or conflicting.
example: The assistant says the supplied documents do not answer the question and suggests a human follow-up.
commonMistake: Asking for a confident tone when the evidence is weak.
learningTip: A clear unknown is often safer and more useful than a polished guess.

definition: An authoritative source close to the original event, rule, data, or decision being checked.
example: The official regulation rather than an unsourced summary of the regulation.
commonMistake: Using any search result as equally authoritative.
learningTip: Match the source authority to the stakes of the decision.

definition: A systematic pattern that can produce unfair or unequal outcomes for people or groups.
example: A screening process rejects qualified applicants from one group more often than others.
commonMistake: Looking only at the model and ignoring data, labels, objectives, or deployment context.
learningTip: Trace where data came from, what it measures, who is represented, and who bears errors.

definition: A meaningful human ability to review, question, correct, or stop an AI-supported process.
example: A qualified reviewer checks a high-impact recommendation and can reject it with a reason.
commonMistake: Putting a person in the final step without giving them time, information, or authority to intervene.
learningTip: Check whether the human role has real decision power and clear accountability.

definition: Making an AI system's role, limits, data use, and decision process understandable to relevant people.
example: Applicants are told that an automated recommendation supports review and how to request correction.
commonMistake: Publishing technical details while hiding the practical effect on people.
learningTip: Explain what the system does, what it cannot do, and how people can challenge an outcome.

definition: Collecting and using only the personal or sensitive data needed for a clearly defined purpose.
example: A tutoring tool uses a learner's selected level rather than collecting unrelated identity details.
commonMistake: Collecting extra data because it might be useful someday.
learningTip: For every field, ask why it is needed, who can access it, and when it should be deleted.

definition: The agreed questions or measures used to judge whether an AI output meets the task's needs.
example: A support team checks factual accuracy, policy fit, tone, privacy, and escalation needs.
commonMistake: Using one generic score for every task and risk level.
learningTip: Start with success criteria, then add checks for likely errors and harms.

definition: A trusted reference, label, or expert judgment used as a comparison point during evaluation.
example: Comparing an AI summary with the approved source notes and a subject-matter review.
commonMistake: Treating the model's own explanation as ground truth.
learningTip: Choose a reference that is authoritative for the task and current enough to matter.

definition: The degree to which an output includes all material information required by the task.
example: A policy summary preserves exceptions, deadlines, and approval requirements.
commonMistake: Assuming a short response is complete because it is easy to read.
learningTip: Create a checklist from the task and mark omissions separately from factual errors.

definition: Checking whether an output could create harm, expose private information, or encourage unsafe action.
example: A reviewer removes a suggestion to share a customer's account number in a public reply.
commonMistake: Treating safety as separate from quality and checking it only when something goes wrong.
learningTip: Add safety and privacy checks before an AI output can trigger an action.

definition: A workflow that retrieves relevant source content and supplies it to a language model before generation.
example: A support assistant searches approved help articles before drafting a customer reply.
commonMistake: Thinking retrieval permanently retrains the language model for every question.
learningTip: Separate the search step, the supplied context, and the generation step when explaining RAG.

definition: Using relevant evidence or source material to anchor a generated answer.
example: A response quotes the current handbook section used to answer a policy question.
commonMistake: Assuming supplied context is automatically correct or relevant.
learningTip: Evaluate source authority, freshness, retrieval relevance, and whether the answer matches the source.

definition: The search or ranking component that selects documents or passages relevant to a query.
example: A semantic search service returns three handbook sections related to parental leave.
commonMistake: Treating the top search result as authoritative without checking its version or source.
learningTip: Track source metadata such as owner, date, approval status, and section identity.

definition: How current and valid retrieved material is for the question being answered.
example: The current approved handbook replaces a retired policy page in the search index.
commonMistake: Keeping old documents searchable without labels or update rules.
learningTip: Use version and approval metadata to prefer current sources and expose conflicts.

definition: A bounded process that connects inputs, AI steps, checks, decisions, outputs, and feedback.
example: Classify a request, retrieve approved content, draft a response, validate it, and escalate uncertain cases.
commonMistake: Treating one impressive prompt as a complete production workflow.
learningTip: Map what happens before and after generation, including failure and human handoff paths.

definition: A workflow design in which a person reviews, approves, corrects, or handles selected AI cases.
example: A specialist reviews billing disputes before an AI-drafted reply is sent.
commonMistake: Adding a human step without giving the reviewer authority or enough context.
learningTip: Define which cases trigger review and what the reviewer can change or stop.

definition: A measurable condition that describes whether a workflow is achieving its intended outcome.
example: At least 95% of approved replies contain the required policy reference without exposing private data.
commonMistake: Measuring only speed while ignoring quality, safety, or user outcomes.
learningTip: Pair efficiency measures with accuracy, safety, and escalation measures that reflect the real goal.

definition: Routing an uncertain, risky, or exceptional case to a person or a safer process.
example: A support workflow sends privacy-sensitive requests to a trained specialist.
commonMistake: Treating escalation as a failure instead of a deliberate safety control.
learningTip: Define observable triggers for escalation before the workflow is deployed.
